blogs.title: No Private Right to ‘Average Daily Wage’ Penalties Under MPWA § 181.101
blogs.description: The Eighth Circuit reads Minnesota’s wage statute to reserve average-daily-wage penalties to the Commissioner of Labor and Industry, not private plaintiffs. The post unpacks the statutory text of §§ 181.101 and 181.171, the court’s use of comparative statutory structure (contrasting §§ 181.13 and 181.14), and Milner’s role, and explains the practical consequences: employees can sue for unpaid wages, but penalty leverage runs through the agency after a formal demand. It also assesses what this means for plaintiffs’ litigation strategy and employer compliance in Minnesota.

blogs.title: Penalties Without Payout: Standing and Mootness for MFLSA Civil Penalties Payable Only to the State
blogs.description: Vacating summary judgment, the Eighth Circuit remands to determine whether a private plaintiff has a live Article III controversy when wages and liquidated damages are paid and only civil penalties—payable to the Commissioner—remain. This post analyzes the court’s reliance on Laidlaw’s deterrence rationale, the voluntary-cessation doctrine, and Town of Chester’s claim-by-claim standing requirement, alongside Judge Kobes’s concurrence questioning Laidlaw’s fit outside environmental statutes. It maps possible outcomes on remand and the unresolved question whether the MFLSA’s scheme contemplates private pursuit of state-payable penalties.

blogs.title: When Paying Up Isn’t the End: Voluntary Cessation, ‘Pick-Offs,’ and Injunctive Relief in Wage Cases
blogs.description: Consilio’s payment of all overtime and liquidated damages didn’t fully moot the case because civil penalties and potential injunctive relief loomed—yet the plaintiff’s shifting request for an injunction wasn’t preserved. This piece situates the opinion within the post–Campbell-Ewald landscape, explains how Laidlaw’s voluntary-cessation doctrine can keep claims alive if an unlawful policy persists, and offers practical guidance: plead ongoing violations and injunctive remedies clearly and early, build a record on current policies, and anticipate defendants’ tender strategies aimed at truncating class and deterrence claims.

blogs.title: Preservation Matters: The MWTA Claim and the Perils of Changing Remedies Midstream
blogs.description: The court affirms dismissal of the Minnesota Wage Theft Act claim and declines to consider a newly framed request for injunctive relief raised at summary judgment. This post examines the opinion’s waiver and forfeiture analysis (including reliance on InfoDeli and Rule 28), the need to amend pleadings under Rule 15 to pursue different injunctive remedies, and lessons for practitioners on issue preservation, remedy alignment with statutory authority, and briefing discipline on appeal.

blogs.title: Agency-Centered Penalties and Private Enforcement in Minnesota Wage Law After Cohen
blogs.description: By holding that § 181.101 penalties run exclusively through the Commissioner, the Eighth Circuit underscores Minnesota’s mixed enforcement model: private actions for wages, agency control over key penalties. This post situates the decision within broader debates about private attorney-general mechanisms, compares Minnesota’s design to more expansive private-penalty regimes (e.g., PAGA-style systems), and assesses policy tradeoffs in channeling deterrence through administrative demand-and-collection processes rather than private suits.

blogs.title: Erie, Certification, and Reading State Wage Statutes in Federal Court
blogs.description: Relying on Minnesota Supreme Court precedents like Milner and Allan, the Eighth Circuit treated § 181.101’s penalty pathway as clear. This post examines whether the panel’s approach leaves any room for state-law ambiguity, the potential for (and prudence of) certification to the Minnesota Supreme Court on private access to penalties, and how federal courts should navigate statutory schemes where remedies are split between agency and private hands.
